麦当劳的穷鬼套餐又多给我送了两块麦乐鸡。

突然想到lxl那天说她是百分之七十五幸运女孩。虽然不知道我是百分之多少，但总感觉不应该把运气浪费在这种奇怪的事情上。于是我假装没看见多出来的那两块麦乐鸡，冷血的把它们送进了垃圾桶。即便如此，还是很倒霉的发现mimi门口排着动都不动的长队。我翻了个白眼头也不回的就走了。
突然发现其实百分之七十五幸运女孩也是百分之二十五倒霉女孩。作为bayesianist，我觉得其实我应该是百分之五十幸运女孩。因为对于任何事情都可以说，狗屁运不运的，概率不都是五十对五十？（formal epistemology）
正常人应该在一个幸运中性测度下幸运值为0，相比之下lxl比我们多了25点，她简直是超人。在这个幸运中性的世界里我倒霉的遇上了mimi的长队，但又幸运的发现madison fare今天有开心果酱。但其实后者也弥补不了前者的倒霉。所以我猜回到真实世界里，一件事消耗我多少幸运值和其概率负相关。这几天最幸运的是去考试的路上看到两只狗在雪地里打架。当时戴着耳机，回看视频才发现竟然还有配乐，配合这画面特别好笑。

小狗在雪地里打架还有bgm的概率应该比开出6块麦乐鸡还低。但我愿意他们消耗掉我更多幸运值，他们应得的。

blog_publication/Dec1_2025.content:
总有一些歌是反季节的。
比如打雷就应该夏天听，但我经常听到the next best American record想起高三的冬天。我在虹桥那个自习室的小隔间里听着歌，做没完没了的圆锥曲线和导数大题，然后不时发呆，望着被雨夹雪笼罩的灰蒙蒙的南京城北。阴冷的日子里我脑中全是六个月后的夏天，那时我刚考完高考，会在梧桐树荫下听见蝉鸣，会在湛蓝的海水旁边狂奔，会被热浪赶走身上所有的潮湿。只有在冬天我会忘了南京的夏天有多毒辣。
印象里北京也是灰蒙蒙的，但是不知为何北京的灰蒙蒙比南京多出点古色古香的意趣。去年感恩节我在前门大街游荡，想起ljc说有一条杨梅竹斜街上很多咖啡店挺有情调。咖啡店在老房子里，踏上嘎吱嘎吱响的红漆木楼梯，透过二楼的窗子能看见周围房子斑驳的屋檐和砖缝里的青苔。楼上一个人没有，老板一边招呼我随便坐一边打开暖气。音响里来来回回就三首歌，我一首都叫不上名字。但我只搜了这一首take me home，感觉它慵懒的声音竟然和此情此景有种诡异的契合。
这首歌更适合放在沙滩边的躺椅上，午后的阳光微微刺痛着裸露的肌肤，在海浪声中睁开睡意朦胧的双眼，然后移开脸上的遮阳帽。海风把沙粒卷到小腿上，逗得人痒痒的，引诱你在滚烫的沙粒上踩下几个脚印。甜品吃完了，咖啡见底了，二楼渐渐暖和起来了，音响里还是这三首歌。再一次循环到take me home的时候沙滩的图景消失了，我突然觉得这首歌如果没有开头的海浪声也很适合冬天。适合在窝在熊熊燃烧的壁炉旁边的沙发里，看着窗外大雪纷飞，慢慢睡着。
南京已经很久没有下过漫天飞舞的大雪了，更别提上海。请不要再让我在黏黏的雨夹雪里发霉了。希望今年纽约雪真的很大。

blog_publication/Dec9_2025.content:
在大家围在桌前聊到五点钟的那个夜晚我开始感到不安。我知道的，幸福在其达到极点的那一刻起就在漫漫消散。我突然意识到没有什么理所应当的事，并不会一敲隔壁的门lyh就会来打游戏，也不会在群里面一喊mia就上来打牌。
可惜三年前在那些溜进媛的画室的晚上我没意识到这点，总感觉能在画室来去自如的日子会一直继续下去。从小到大搬了那么多次家，我本以为不会再对一个地方产生特别的情愫了。
寻常的一天我或许会三次出现在画室。中午和dxy从食堂溜达到超市，再从超市慢慢溜达到实验楼。走上三楼，推开画室的门，看到yjc和xxy在我买的懒人沙发上卿卿我我，另一边媛在躺椅上翘着二郎腿玩游戏。下午最后一节课后，在画室盥洗室的窗边吃着外卖，默默注视着楼下的天桥。来来往往的人群没有一个人抬头往我这看。每个体育课下课我们走过天桥，只有我会边和别人讲话边不自觉的瞟画室一眼，看到那扇窗户隐于梧桐树梢后。这时我会因为画室而感到无比幸福。这是只属于我们几个人的地方，我们在校园里面却又游离于学校之外，能如局外人一样恣意妄为。六点二十，我们假装抱作业去办公室看一眼谭林在不在，不在的话就回到画室，一待待到九点。
毕业后，光是收拾画室里我自己的东西就收拾了半天。书，花瓶，香薰，衣服帽子堆了满满一纸箱。我和媛说其实这些都可以留在这的。她说你拿走吧，这里要重新装修了。我觉着心里空落落的。
从开足冷气的画室走出来，瞬间被热浪包裹，眼镜起了厚厚一层雾，从此关于这里的记忆变得越来越模糊，只有那天阳光刺痛肌肤的感觉依旧清晰。抱着纸盒走到校门口天桥下，再看往画室的方向。终于，我意识到即使再依恋这里它也不会属于我。即使没有毕业这里也会装修，今天我也会抱着一堆东西站在这里，不会理所应当的每天坐在画室里发呆，看书，和朋友有说有笑。我只是画室的一个过客而已。
空荡荡的大街上只剩我一个人站在那等车。我听见蝉在死命的尖叫，中山北路上工地哒哒哒的钻地声，远处汽车呼啸而过，但世界却显得格外寂静。我想起周末一个人翻进画室的午后，和朋友在画室吃的蛋糕，和媛在画室一起筹备的校庆画展。我想起很久很久以前就想过在毕业那天和朋友们在画室拍一张拍立得，连每个人会做什么动作我都想好了。可能大家会围在懒人沙发前面，王子枫会抱着他的吉他，yjc会和xxy一起比个心，可能dxy和wsy一个人比耶一个人竖个大拇指。但那天媛竟然没来上班，再后来王子枫先回了扬州，之后再怎么凑人都不齐了。于是这个想法继续被埋在心底，但我知道再也回不去从前的画室了。南京的六月好热好热，太阳照的沥青路面都开始反光，上方的空气泛起波纹。我都不知道是我真的没有哭还是泪水一涌出眼眶就蒸发了。
一年后媛说画室装修好了，要不要回来看看。原来乱糟糟的画室变成了美术教室，看上去很高级，门上还有个指纹锁。媛苦笑了一下把门打开，说现在没有人会像我们一样动不动跑画室来了，但办公室还是能招待一下人的。我问我的懒人沙发呢，她说太脏了扔了，但你还落了两本书在我这。我说你留着吧，盗版的。之后很多次回到nsfz，但再也没去过那里。









zyg说所有关系都是阶段性的，有人则不以为然。我知道她也很珍惜她的朋友，但我就是缺少那种不再觉得失去是舍不得的豁达。至少从这个角度来说，我相当死脑筋。
rzh告诉我我们宿舍被分到拉法叶，和很多人分开的时候，James Walsh正在讲defining truth的问题。PA里没有办法定义PA的truth predicate，只能在SA里定义；SA也不能定义自己的truth predicate，所有formal system的truth都只能在一个更强的系统里定义。James说可能乐观的人会说这样的truth hierarchy太好了，所有问题都有一个更强的系统解决；而悲观的人会说但是所有的系统里都会有不能定义truth的问题。这话有种苏轼写赤壁赋的意趣，自其变者而观之、自其不变者而观之。很明显我是那个悲观的人，总觉得世界千疮百孔。比如尽管我知道这不可能，但我总是幼稚的幻想拥有永恒的生命，来去自如的空间，和永远不会结束的友谊。
寒冷的天气里人总是会格外多愁善感，为自己那些永远不会实现的幻想感到痛楚。ccz说可是这些不在这个季节也存在啊。我说不同季节有不同的事要去难过。春天要在树下感慨生命短暂无常，夏天要在湿闷的空气中追悔错误的决定，秋天要在纷飞的落叶中忍住眼泪告别。他说这么悲观不完蛋了，不如肤浅一点。我本来就很肤浅，十分钟前难过的事其实是黑五没钱买衣服。
与其说是悲观，可能我只是觉得豁达的态度没有吸引力。高中时赤壁赋客说的话记得清清楚楚，苏子曰那一段怎么也背不下来。寄蜉蝣于天地，渺沧海之一粟的悲凉十分显而易见，但是自其不变者而观之，则物与我皆无尽也这句话和后面几句在我看来近乎狗屁不通。zyg觉得苏子说的话很好，惟江上之清风，与山间之明月，耳得之而为声，目遇之而成色，取之无禁，用之不竭，写的极美。其实这段话并没有反驳客之所言。纵使山间明月和江上清风取之不尽用之不竭，曹孟德仍旧不会出现在千年后的赤壁，客，苏子，我，你，所有人都寄蜉蝣于天地，秒沧海之一粟。毋庸置疑，苏轼自己也知道这一点，那为什么还要写后面那些自我安慰的话。诚然，如果把后面苏子的话删掉，我实在想象不到赤壁赋会如何成为不朽的文章，总得有人唱唱反调才有意思。jt说这辈子都已经这么累了，不安慰一下还让不让人活了。
或许他的确认为这是哀吾生之须臾的解决方法而不只是自我安慰。苏轼的蜀学驳杂不纯，混淆孔老之道，如果是虚无寂灭之学，就不得不承认世界变幻无常；可老庄的寂灭之道又认定世界存在源头一样的“一”，或许藏于江上清风和山间明月，让人从现象回到本源，在刹那间领悟到永恒。
我并不认为世界存在一个可触及的，可被感受的本源。退一万步来说，即使真的能从noumenal的世界里领悟到永恒，那也和我们所在的现象世界没有半毛钱关系。我一直不理解，人们为什么要想方设法说服自己明明很悲哀的事情并不悲哀，为什么要给无法解决的问题强塞一个解决方案，最后结局是几乎千篇一律的豁然开朗。我总觉得悲伤更具有审美价值。挟飞仙以遨游，抱明月而长终。知不可乎骤得，托遗响于悲风。如此物哀之美，远胜能领悟到永恒的虚幻的希望。
如果是一篇作文的话或许该从这里开始转折了，写下一个大大的然而，最后像赤壁赋一样豁然开朗。但显然这不是作文，我也不是苏轼。
如同他在一个生之须臾的现象世界和无穷无尽的本源世界里来回徘徊一样，我也总是在一种哀伤与迷恋哀伤的心境中举棋不定。但这样似乎更糟了。关于离别，我也只能在叹息中束手无策。









繁花舞台剧第二季里有个桥段，阿宝父亲和同事欧阳先生平反，让阿宝去找以前一位朋友。黎老师是一个头发花白的老奶奶，双目失明，坐在椅子上和阿宝说以前的她和她先生（读书人）的事情。


                  
                  Quote
                  
                

英伦首相艾德礼宣布，全国放两天假，美国也放两天假。中国庆祝三天，政府部门，放假一天。这天夜里，我跟了读书人与先生，三个人，开开心心荡马路，满城箫鼓，大小报纸登了杜鲁门的演说，自今日起吾人將進入一新紀元。
霞飞路，真是人声鼎沸呀，亚尔培路，就是现在陕西路淮海路口，男女白俄跳舞，拉手风琴，集中营关了四年的英侨，美侨，全部放出来了，成群结队，到霞飞路游行，我清清爽爽听见，有一个美侨唱《莉莉玛莲》，雾气里一切遮掩，我还是凭窗佇立，莉莉玛莲，莉莉玛莲。我的眼泪，就落下来了，这天夜里，三个人，多高兴呀，随便推开西区一扇陌生大铁门，一幢大洋房，当时上海，有多少空洋房呀，人去楼空，三个人摸进去，开电灯，橱里摆满洋酒，我到大厅开了留声机，居然寻到《和莉瑪蓮》德文唱片，大家就听，唱，跳，我就哭了，这一夜，我吃了多少酒呀，三个人跑到花园草地上转圈子，空气真好，甘凉清芬，我开口就唱，莉莉玛莲。眼泪就落下来，是为高兴哭的，上海呀真是光复了，上海真的是亮了，闹到了深更半夜，唉，读书人跟欧阳先生，醉得人事不醒，直到第二天下午，大家离开。
……
后来又是兵临上海了，读书人对我讲，黎黎，天又要亮了，不是微亮，马上大放光明了，光明世界，马上就要到了。后来却等来彩云难驻，明月空圆了，全部变了。捉了不少人，形势严峻，手铐用麻袋来装。


于是黎老师再也没见过她的先生和欧阳。廿几年后，已是阴阳两隔。黎老师叹息，灯暗。泪水止不住的流淌出来。
没关系的，离别就是伤感的，想哭就哭吧。

blog_publication/Nov9_2025.title: Nov9_2025
blog_publication/Nov9_2025.content:
放学后趴在走廊的栏杆上，透过几乎是光秃秃的梧桐树枝向西望去。太阳已经不见了，只剩微微泛红的天边和不远处工地的剪影。我忽然意识到已经立冬了。
11月的风恶毒地钻进我的领子。我只能将双手死死抱在胸前，眯着眼睛往后门走去。后门那时没有因为疫情封闭，学生来来往往，远比现在热闹。我一直对饺子无感，可我竟然在主动找能吃饺子的地方。这甚至是我第一次听说立冬有这个习俗。其实吃什么都无所谓，只是觉得该好好庆祝一下冬天。即使冬天把我冻的瑟瑟发抖我也喜欢冬天，喜欢把自己挪回室内时身体重新焕发生机的感觉，喜欢大脑晕乎乎的幸福的感觉。
我刻意避开了平时会去的那家馄炖店，因为我知道走上二楼一定会看到那群男的在玩原神，多少会有点扫兴。于是我多往前走了两步，去了一家很少去的面馆。我张望了一下，大家在面馆里都点的是饺子。
五年后，在一个离南京十万八千里的城市里几人在没头没脑的说寒假要做的事。dzp说，冬天不就应该除了谈恋爱什么事情都不干吗。我愣了两秒。好久没有从任何一个朋友嘴巴里听到过这么正确的话了。我由衷的认为她是天才。她说这话的时候正牵着男朋友在UPenn的草坪上走着，落叶在脚下发出嘎吱嘎吱的声响。
nsfz那条鹅卵石小路一到十月也会铺满褐色的梧桐叶，那些叶子像秋天自身一般脆弱。九点半，晚自习课间的喧闹声渐渐归于平静，谁在那里踩一脚梧桐叶，六楼的窗边都能听的一清二楚。如果传来的是急促的刺啦刺啦声，可能是老师正在往班上赶；但如果每一声都拖的长长的，让你感受到叶子正沿着纹路碎裂开来，那一定是还在私会的欲说还休的情侣。
而此时此刻这样面馆里坐满了这样的情侣，狭小的店面里只有我突兀的站在那。我鼓起勇气想去问一对情侣能不能拼个桌，还没开口椅子就被老板一把薅起来，递给门口另外一对。
几年后我和王子枫专程去看了眼后门，那里萧条的已和往日是两幅模样。
聊起这家面馆，他也说老板的态度很差，总是忽视一个人来的顾客。我说到那个立冬的晚上，说到我经常幻想在放学的傍晚有人能和我并肩走着，从炸鸡店游荡到回龙桥的花店，从未名湖走到标本林，看路灯把我们的影子拉得很长很长。
王子枫说唉冬天。他说不出来冬天应该谈恋爱以外什么事都不干这种话。但这不是因为他不是天才，只是他已经很久没有和人一起走过那条铺满梧桐叶的鹅卵石小路了。

blog_publication/Oct26_2025.title: Oct26_2025
blog_publication/Oct26_2025.content:
我在maudlin讲fact, fiction, and forecast的时候走了神，因为我课前根本没看这本书。他的小狗正屁股对着我，我开始思考它什么时候屁颠屁颠跑过来趴我腿上。它毛茸茸的，很像今天的云朵。上学路上我幽怨的盯着天空，想为什么好天气永远在上学的时候出现。
恍惚间听到老师说在他想来世界有种最坏的可能，可能一切只存在了一秒，在此之前所有记忆全是幻觉。
听上去是个很老掉牙的skepticism问题，毕竟这本书就是个重生版的hume。我不知道怎么反驳他。我想这确实有可能，毕竟一秒钟前我在白日做梦，或许世界诞生于梦醒时分，梦到的东西只是世界解的initial condition。我很讨厌康德用一些超自然和自己不承认是心理学的心理学去反驳他的做法。
maudlin说拒绝这种可能也不实用。哪怕世界在此刻才开始运转，也不会影响任何我们对世界的认知，物理学的定律不会因此发生变化，历史书也不会改写。我们只是不知道怎么证明这一切确实存在。
而此时此刻maudlin的小狗真钻到了我身边。真是遗憾，抚摸它脑袋时这种触手可及的真实感也没法被证明。承认这一切的真实性似乎不可避免的要多一些ontology上的负担。
我想如果这一切都是真实的话，今天我像往常所有的周二一样九点半被闹钟吵醒，睁开右眼按掉闹钟，继续昏迷到十点半。我在街角的deli慢悠悠的吃完三明治后准备连着第四周迟到，因为这样电梯门在三楼一打开就能看到maudlin的小狗在门口迎接我。我会在门口反复摩挲两遍它毛茸茸的脑袋再进教室。可惜今天失策了，他到的比我还晚。
其实今天我也不是十点半起的床，可能早了十分钟。醒来时太阳在云层中不时探头，光线透过百叶窗让房间不停明暗交替。我想起刚才做的梦，我在没有尽头的荒原里飞奔，穿过白昼，穿过黑夜，穿过光明，穿过阴霾。我知道这不可能是真的，但是我也不知道该如何证明。
我想起王二想变成天上忽明忽暗的云，但我没有这种想法。这种话只有诗人才说得出来，我不是诗人。我只会想一些不切实际的问题。

高二，疫情在家，我跟爹妈说想玩胶片。他们说你不该抓紧时间学习吗。我偷偷花了两百买了一个kiss1还有最便宜的gold200。我学着b站上的文艺逼去回龙桥和双门楼那里的小巷子里去扫街，去拍破破烂烂的房屋和意义不明的废墟。我知道我拍的乱七八糟但我很开心。我想我会一直拍下去，说不定哪天我会成为森山大道。
我的父母很少说学生最重要的是学习这种话，也很少管我成绩怎么样。但是这次他们说拍照的事可以以后再搞，上了大学有的是时间。我哭了。我说我不想把喜欢的事情拖到以后，以后说不定就不喜欢了，我不想我的热情被时间耗费掉。我和我爹说，你说你以前就很想学摄影，长大了有钱了买了个相机。现在你有钱了，但一年你又把相机拿出来过几次呢。
当时我十七岁，其实想的不是等自己有钱了买相机我爹管不着了，而是我能不能活到高考结束。就像即便把相机攥的再紧也会担心它掉到地上一样，我也好担心哪天我也会突然这样支离破碎。我想，在活着的时候能拍出流芳百世的作品也算死而无憾了。我心中有好多想要记录下的画面。我想拍nsfz在三月的某天会从天而降的桃花雨，想拍鹅卵石小路上的银杏叶，想拍长椅上的猫咪和栏杆缝隙中的阳光。
如同其他无数次的争吵一样这次也是不了了之。但不知道是不是他们说的话让我有些动摇，我也放弃了在街上拍那些不知所以的照片。但我还在幻想着，或许只是因为时间不够，或许只是我被高考搞得心烦意乱。我买了个gr1，还觉得自己身体里有个森山大道。
但是gr1只拍了一卷。那个三月我也没有看到桃花雨。
我买了s5，第一个学期其实根本没拍过。摆脱了高考照样有其他事情让我心烦意乱。而且我也没时间，有时间也没力气拿起相机了。我高中的时候还是太聪明了，以后什么吊样都能料想的到。所以我一整年满意的作品都凑不出一个九宫格。我现在知道我没有死在高考前，但我也不会成为森山大道了。

math_logic
Introduction and \Sigma_1, \Pi_1, \Delta_0 formulas
The \Delta_0 formulas of PA are those in which all quantifiers are bounded. More precisely:

every atomic formula is \Delta_0
if F and G are \Delta_0, then \sim F and F\supset G are \Delta_0
if F is \Delta_0, v a variable, t a term not containing v, then \forall v(v\le t\supset F) is \Delta_0.
That means \Delta_0 formulas are bounded.

A \Sigma_1 formula is those \exists v_{1}\exists v_{2}\dots\exists v_{n}F, where F is \Delta_0. Symmetrically, a \Pi_1 formula is \forall v_{1}\dots\forall v_{n} F where F is \Delta_0. So \Sigma_1 and \Pi_{1} are unbounded. Notice that the negation of a \Sigma_{1} is \Pi_{1}. Look at several formulas we met before: Gödel sentence G is \Pi_1, Prov(y) is \Sigma_{1}, (Con) is \Pi_{1}.
This document aims to show the strengthened representability theorem.
\Delta_0 completeness
TODO
\Sigma_1 completeness and \Sigma_1 soundness
A \Sigma_1 sentence \exists v_{1}\dots\exists v_{n}F(v_{1},\dots,v_{n}) is true iff there exists numbers k_{1},\dots,k_{m} such that F(\bar k_{1},\dots,\bar k_{m}) is true (we will talk about truth in another doc). By \Delta_{0} completeness we know that if F(\bar k_{1},\dots,\bar k_{m}) holds then \vdash F(\bar k_{1},\dots,\bar k_{m}), so \vdash \exists k_{1},\dots,\exists v_{m}F(\bar k_{1},\dots,\bar k_{m}) by existential generalization. Thus PA is \Sigma_{1}complete, i.e. **all true \Sigma_{1} sentences are derivable. **
Note that we cannot claim any stronger: we may not be able to refute a false \Sigma_1 sentence, for its negation is \Pi_{1}.
The converse property to \Sigma_{1} completeness is called \Sigma_{1} soundness: every derivable \Sigma_{1} sentence is true. It implies that if \exists x F(x) is a derivable \Sigma_{1} sentence then some numerical instance F(\bar k) is derivable. For if \exists x F(x) is true, then F(\bar k) is true for some k, so that \vdash F(\bar k) by \Sigma_{1} completeness. Note that the \Sigma_{1} soundness also implies \Sigma_{1} consistency.
Proof of representability
To show every primitive recursive function is numeralwise representable, we shall show three things:

basic functions (constant, identity, successor function) are numeralwise representable
representability is closed under composition
representability is closed under recursion

Consider a representative case: a two-place function \varphi defined by
\begin{aligned}
\varphi(n,0) &= \theta(n)\\
\varphi(n,k+1) &= \psi(n,k,\varphi(n,k))
\end{aligned}
where \theta and \psi are functions know to be representable.

phil_public/Gödel_incompleteness.content:
math_logic PA
This document is based on Goldfarb’s Note.
Introduction
The theorems originated in the objection to Hilbert’s project of axiomatizing arithmetic. Hilbert was trying to build a Euclidean-like arithmetic formal system (PA) that could be built up by several axioms and prove all the true propositions by deduction. So we need to show that PA is (1) syntactically complete: for all well-formed formulas in PA, we can either prove it or refute it; (2) consistent: PA does not prove \sim P if it proves P.
However, this beautiful picture is rejected by Gödel’s proof of his first and second incompleteness theorems corresponding to the completeness and consistency of PA. The first theorem claims that if PA is \omega-consistent, then there are some well-formed formulas that you can neither prove nor refute. The second theorem claims that if PA is consistent, you cannot prove PA is consistent in PA.
The intuition of the first incompleteness theorem is to construct such a formula G as an analogue of the Liar paradox that
\vdash G\equiv \ulcorner G\urcorner \text{ is not provable in PA}
By constructing such a self-reference and discussing \vdash G and \nvdash G. We can arrive at the absurdity that PA is inconsistent, which contradicts our premise. The key to the proof is using diag to construct the self-reference and define the provability predicates with gödelization.
In this document, I will first prove the fixed-point lemma and prove the first incompleteness theorem as a corollary.
The intuition of the second incompleteness theorem is an analogue of Curry’s paradox. Suppose there is a sentence that says, “If this sentence is true, then Santa Claus exists.” Consider the following deduction:

Suppose that if this sentence is true, then Santa Claus exists.

Suppose this sentence is true

Santa Claus exists (MP)


If this sentence is true, then Santa Claus exists. (Sub-conclusion from the supposition)


This sentence is true (we have proved it under the supposition)
Santa Claus exists (MP)
This paradox leads to the conclusion that we can prove everything. The error still lies in self-reference. The Lob’s theorem is an analogue to this paradox, replacing “true” with “provable”.

Gödelization
Gödel numbering
Here is a table for PA symbols:





































































PA symbolsGödel numbers"0"1"S"2"+"3"\times"4"="5"\sim"6"\supset"7"\forall"8"("9")"10"x"17other varaiblesodd numbers > 17The PA symbols have there unique gödel number, and the mapping is denoted by \Gamma. e.g. \Gamma(0) = 1For every PA formula, the Gödel number of the sequence is encoded by the prime number product with the powers be the Gödel numbers of the symbol. The mapping is denoted by \gamma. e.g.\gamma(\sim S0 = 0) = 2^{6}\cdot3^{2}\cdot5^{1}\cdot7^{5}\cdot 11^{1}

Numeralwise representability
(we will revisit this part in Formalizing_primitive_recursion, and here we won’t give a proof but just conclusions).
Now we shall build a link between the informal maths in the previous two parts with the formal system. We take 2-place relations for vividness and in fact, that is as far as we would go. A formula F(x,y) in language of PA whose only free variable are x and y, numeralwise represents the relation R iff for all integers k and n,
\begin{aligned}
&\text{if } R(k,n)\text{ then }\vdash F(\bar k,\bar n)\\
&\text{if } \overline R(k,n)\text{ then }\vdash \sim F(\bar k,\bar n).
\end{aligned}
Here \overline R means the relation R doesn’t hold. \bar k and \bar n means the numeral of k and n (like there is no "2" in L_{PA}, its numeral is SS0). For example, consider the identity relation x=y (this is informal). To show this we must show that for any numeral \bar k and \bar n, if k = n (informal), then \vdash \bar k = \bar n (formal, in PA); if k \neq n, then \vdash \sim \bar k = \bar n.
We also want to formulate a notion of numeralwise representation for functions. Here, we want PA to capture the fact that a function has a unique value for each argument.
Let \varphi be an 2-place function from numbers to numbers (informal). A formula F(x,y,z) numeralwise represents the function \varphi in PA iff for all numbers m,n and q such that \varphi(m,n) = q
\vdash F(\bar m,\bar n,z)\equiv z = \bar q.

Notice that \varphi doesn’t have to be two place. Here it is just for the sake of convenience. A one-place function \phi can be numeralwise represented by F iff for all numbers p and q such that \phi(p) = q, we have
\vdash F(\bar p,z)\equiv z=\bar q.

 It requires only that the formalization of “pointwise facts” about the relation or function be derivable in PA: for all particular arguments, whether the relation holds or not, and for all particular arguments, what the value of the function is and that it is the only value. For other purposes we might well want to require more, for example, that formalizations of general laws that the relation or the function obeys be derivable in PA. (Goldfarb 37)



                  
                   Representability Theorem
                  
                

Every primitive recursive relation and function is numeralwise representable in PA.


Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem
Fixed-point Lemma
This is the most exciting part of Gödel’s proof. Here I will give a clean proof.


                  
                   Fixed Point Lemma
                  
                

Let F(y) be any formula in L_{PA}. Then there is a formula H such that \vdash H\equiv F(\bar m), where m is the Gödel number of H.


Proof:
Consider the formula F'(y).
\forall z \bigg(\Delta(y,z)\supset F(z)\bigg),
where F(x) can be any formula, and \Delta(y,z) numeralwise represents the relation of diag, i.e.:
\begin{aligned}
&\text{if } diag(y) = z\quad\text{ then }\vdash \Delta(\bar y,\bar z)\\
&\text{if } diag(y) \neq z\quad \text{ then }\vdash \sim \Delta(\bar y,\bar z).
\end{aligned}
Now we let k = \gamma\big(F'(y)\big), and H be F'(\bar k). Let m = \gamma(H) = \gamma\big(F'(\bar k)\big).
By the definition of diag, we know that diag(k) = m.
(recall that diag is replacing the gödel number of y with the gödel number of the sentence itself)
F'(\bar k) is \forall z\bigg(\Delta(\bar k,z)\supset F(z)\bigg). Recall that since the function diag numeralwise represents \Delta, then
\vdash \Delta (\bar k,z)\equiv z = \bar m.
So by truth-functional logic, F'(\bar k) is provably the same as \forall z\bigg(z = \bar m\supset F(z)\bigg), which is truth-functionally equivalent to F(\bar m). So we proved that
\vdash F'(\bar k)\equiv F(\bar m)
Now observe the definition of m, it is the Gödel number of F'(\bar k), i.e. H. In conclusion:
\vdash H\equiv F(\bar m),
where m is the Gödel number of H.
QED

Now introduce a new notation \ulcorner \, \urcorner. For any formula F,
\gamma(\ulcorner F\urcorner) = \overline{\gamma(F)}.
The fixed point lemma is saying that for any formula F(y) there is a formula H that
\vdash H\equiv F(\ulcorner H\urcorner).
Proof of Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem


                  
                   \omega-consistency
                  
                

A theory T is \omega-consistent iff there is no formula \varphi(x) such that:

\vdash_{T}\exists x \varphi(x)
For every n, \vdash_{T} \,\sim\varphi(\bar n)



Note that \omega-consistency is stronger than consistency. Consider this analogue of inconsistency and \omega-inconsistency. Imagine that you are investigating a car accident. For inconsistency, you say: the accident was not caused by a driver and the accident was caused by a driver. For \omega-inconsistency, you say: some driver definitely caused the accident, it is not driver 0, not driver 1, not…
So \omega-consistency allow you to enumerate.

Consider the provable predicates Prov^*(y) which satisfies the two conditions below: 

Adequacy: For any formula F, if \vdash F, then \vdash Prov^*(\ulcorner F\urcorner).
Faithfulness: For any formula F, if \vdash Prov^*(\ulcorner F\urcorner), then \vdash F.
Recall that the derivable predicate D(x,y) which was numeralwise represented by the primitive recursive function Der. We will show that (1) the formula (\exists x)D(x,y) obeys the adequacy rule and if PA is \omega-consistent, then it obeys the faithfulness rule as well.

(1) Suppose \vdash F. By mirroring, there is a k such that Der(k,\gamma(F)). By numeralwise representation, for such a k, \vdash D(\bar k,\ulcorner F\urcorner), then \exists x D(x,\ulcorner F\urcorner). Adequacy fulfills.
(2)Suppose \vdash \exists D(x,\ulcorner F\urcorner). If not \vdash F, then Der(k,\gamma(F)) for no k, so by numeralwise representability, \vdash \sim D(\bar k,\ulcorner F\urcorner) for every k. So if not \vdash F, then PA is \omega-inconsistent. Faithfulness fulfills.
The Proof of Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem is then quite simple.


                  
                   Gödel's first incompleteness theorem
                  
                

If PA is \omega-consistent then there is a sentence G of L_{PA} such that neither G nor \sim G is derivable in PA, and hence PA is syntactically incomplete. (Goldfarb 39)


Proof:
Let G be a fixed point of \sim Prov^*(y). We will show that G is not derivable in PA.

Suppose that \vdash G: Since \vdash G\equiv \sim Prov^*(\ulcorner G\urcorner), then by MP, \vdash \sim Prov^*(\ulcorner G\urcorner). However, by adequacy, \vdash Prov^*(\ulcorner G\urcorner). Thus, PA is inconsistent, so PA is \omega-inconsistent, against our assumption. So \nvdash G.
Suppose that \vdash \sim G: Since \vdash \sim G \equiv Prov^*(\ulcorner G\urcorner) by the contrapositive of the fixed point lemma, then Prov^*(\ulcorner G\urcorner). Then by faithfulness, \vdash G. PA is \omega-inconsistent, against our assumption. So \nvdash \sim G.
QED

Note that \vdash F is opposed to \nvdash F. If \vdash \sim F, then \nvdash F, but not vice versa.
First incompleteness theorem sharpened
Notice that we only need consistency to prove \nvdash G because we only used adequacy there, which was only governed by the property of then Prov^* predicate. Later Barkley Rosser sharpened Gödel’s proof by showing how to prove incompleteness using only consistency. The basic idea was to replace the faithfulness condition with another one, which we shall call the Rosser conidtion. We shall find a provability predicate that fulfiils the adequacy condition and the Rosser condition should be usable in a fixed point argument to establish the incompleteness of PA.

Rosser’s Lemma: Suppose a formula Rov(y) fulfills the following two conditions for all formulas F:

Adequacy: If \vdash F then \vdash Rov(\ulcorner F\urcorner).
Rosser: If \vdash \sim F then \vdash \sim Rov(\ulcorner F\urcorner).

Ler R be a fixed point of \sim Rov(y). If PA is consistent then neither R nor \sim R is derivable.
Sketch of the proof
It is obvious that the proof is quite the same as Gödel’s proof above by discussing \vdash G and \vdash \sim G.

Suppose \vdash G, then \vdash Rov(\ulcorner G\urcorner) by adequacy and \vdash \sim Rov(\ulcorner G\urcorner) by the fixed point. So \nvdash G.
Suppose \vdash \sim G, then \vdash \sim Rov(\ulcorner G\urcorner) by Rosser, and therefore \vdash G by the fixed point. So \nvdash \sim G.

Now the to prove the Theorem it now suﬃces to show the existence of a suitable formula Rov(y). Here Rosser came up with a most ingenious and fertile idea. A refutation of a formula F is a derivation of \sim F. We formalize the following notion, which we dub ‘rovability’:
a formula F is rovable iff there is a derivation of F but no smaller (in gödel number) refutation of F .
We know from the property of \le that (however, it is not trivial, need to prove):

for every integer k, \vdash x\le \bar k\vee\bar k\le x.
for each formula F(x) and each integer k, if F(j) for j = 0,1,\dots, k, then \vdash x\le \bar k\supset F(x).
Now we can define the formula Rov(y). Let Ref be the two-place prmitive recursive relation defined by Ref(k,n)\leftrightarrow Der(k,neg(n)) (the biconditional here means the two are the same in meta language), and let D(x,y) and R(x,y) be numeralwise represent the relation Der and Ref respectively. Let B(x,y) be

D(x,y)\wedge \forall z(z\le x \supset \sim R(z,y)).
Finally let Rov(y) be \exists x B(x,y). B(x,y) satisfies the adequacy condition, for we can check from the numeralwise representability. B(x,y) also satisfies the Rosser condition:
For suppose \vdash \sim F. Thus there is a k such that Ref(k,\gamma(F)), so that \vdash R(\bar k,\ulcorner F\urcorner). Hence \vdash \bar k\le x\supset (\exists z)(z\le x\wedge R(z,\ulcorner F\urcorner)), or equivalently,
\vdash \bar k\le x\supset (\sim\forall z)(z\le x\wedge R(z,\ulcorner F\urcorner))
Now if PA is consistent, then \overline{Der}(j,\gamma(F)) for each j\le k. Hence \vdash \sim D(\bar j,\ulcorner F\urcorner) for j = 0,1,\dots, k. From the second property of "\le" we know that
\vdash x\le \bar k\supset\sim D(x,\ulcorner F\urcorner).
By contrapositive, the first property of \le, and MP we can derive
\vdash\,\sim\bigg( D(x,\ulcorner F\urcorner)\wedge (\forall z)(z\le x\wedge R(z,\ulcorner F\urcorner))\bigg).
By universal generalization we derive \vdash \sim Rov(\ulcorner F\urcorner).
QED


                  
                   Rosser’s Sharpened Incompleteness Theorem
                  
                

If PA is consistent, then PA is not syntactically complete.




Rosser’s Theorem has several interesting consequences. It can be used to show, on the assumption that PA is consistent, the existence of infinitely many logically inequivalent formally undecidable sentences in PA. (A sentence F is formally un-decidable in PA iﬀ F is neither derivable nor refutable in PA.) The argument goes thus. Assume PA consistent. Let R_1 be the Rosser sentence for PA; that is, the fixed point of \sim Rov(y). Thus R_1 is formally undecidable in PA. Now let \text{PA}_1 be the formal system obtained from PA by adding the sentence R_1 as a new axiom. Then \text{PA}_1 is consistent (else \sim R_1 would be derivable in PA, so PA itself would be inconsistent). We may repeat Rosser’s argument for \text{PA}_1: that is, let R_2 be a fixed point of \sim Rov_1(y), where Rov_1(y) is a rovability predicate for the formal system \text{PA}_1. Then R_2 is formally undecidable in PA_1. A fortiori, R_2 is formally undecidable in PA. Now let \text{PA}_2 be the formal system obtained from \text{PA}_1 by adding R_2 as a new axiom. Again, \text{PA}_2 is consistent. And the Rosser sentence R_3 for the formal system \text{PA}_2 is formally undecidable in \text{PA}_2; a fortiori it is formally undecidable in PA. And so on. (Goldfarb 54)

Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem
Standard provability predicate and consistency predicate
Let (Con) denote the formal expression of consistency (we will enunciate it later). Recall the first incompleteness theorem, G is the Gödel sentence. Number-theoretically speaking, the proof of it is that if the class of Dvbl-numbers has such and such property then \gamma(G) is not a Dvbl-number. We can formalize it in the formula that
(Con)\supset \sim Prov(\ulcorner G\urcorner) \tag{formalized first theorem}
where Prov is the formal expression of expression of derivability. Indeed, by formalizing the proof of the number-theoretic assertion—a proof which, as Gödel emphasized, is purely number-theoretic and uses only simple arithmetical principles—we obtain the derivability in PA of this formula.
But we saw that
\vdash G\equiv \sim Prov(\ulcorner G\urcorner).
Hence
\vdash (Con)\supset G.
We may conclude that if (Con) is derivable in PA, then G can be derived in PA. But then, by the first incompleteness theorem, PA would be inconsistent. So the heart of the proof of the Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem is to show that a formalization of the first incompleteness theorem is derivable. (actually that is just one way and we will not specify on this though it is more straightforward)
Note that the Prov here is not equivalent to the Prov^* we mentioned in the proof of the weaker theorem. The faithfulness is a strong property, so in order to get a more general conclusion (by which I mean do not require the \omega-consistency of PA), we shall define a stand provability predicate. Prov(y) is a standard provability predicate iff it obeys the following conditions:

Adequacy: For each formula F, if \vdash F then \vdash Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner).
Formal Modus Ponens: For all formula F and G, \vdash Prov(\ulcorner F\supset G\urcorner)\supset\big(Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner)\supset Prov(\ulcorner G\urcorner)\big)
Formal Adequacy: For each formula F,\vdash Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner)\supset Prov\big(\ulcorner Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner)\urcorner\big)
Notice a corollary Quick FMP from the definition above: If \vdash F\supset G, then \vdash Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner)\supset  Prov(\ulcorner G\urcorner).


Now consider what the consistency is for: you cannot derive both F and \sim F. Then the representation (Con) should fulfill the following condition:
\text{For each formula }F, \,\,\vdash (Con)\supset \,\sim\big(Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner)\wedge Prov(\ulcorner \sim F\urcorner)\big)\tag{\#}
Recall the explosion rule \vdash (F\wedge\sim F)\supset F' where F' could be any formula (you can prove anything from a contradiction). Then if we can prove anything then not Con. It follows a corollary that for any formula F, \vdash \sim Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner)\supset (Con).
We then can pick any true provability predicate to characterize this, say \sim Prov(\ulcorner S0=0\urcorner). It is straightforward to show it satisfies (\#):
Let F be any formula. We have \vdash F\supset (\sim F\supset S0=0) by truth functional logic. Apply quick FMP we obtain that \vdash Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner)\supset Prov(\ulcorner \sim F\supset S0=0\urcorner). From FMP and truth functional logic we obtain \vdash Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner)\supset \big(Prov(\ulcorner \sim F\urcorner)\supset Prov(\ulcorner S0=0\urcorner)\big). It is truth functionally equivalent to \vdash Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner)\wedge Prov(\ulcorner \sim F\urcorner)\supset Prov(\ulcorner S0=0\urcorner). Take the contrapositive and we get (\#).



                  
                   Gödel's second incompleteness theorem
                  
                

Let (Con) be a sentence of L_{PA} that fulfills condition (\#), where Prov(y) is a standard provability predicate. Then if PA is consistent, (Con) is not derivable in PA.


Proof:
Let G be a fixed point of \sim Prov(y), i.e. \vdash G\equiv \sim Prov(\ulcorner G\urcorner). We have:
\begin{aligned}
&(1)\quad \vdash Prov(\ulcorner G\urcorner)\supset\sim G\qquad\text{contrapositive of the fixed point}\\
&(2)\quad \vdash Prov(\ulcorner Prov(\ulcorner G\urcorner)\urcorner)\supset Prov(\ulcorner \sim G\urcorner)\qquad\text{Quick FMP of (1)}\\
&(3)\quad \vdash Prov(\ulcorner G\urcorner)\supset Prov(\ulcorner Prov(\ulcorner G\urcorner)\urcorner)\qquad\text{Formal Adequacy}\\
&(4)\quad \vdash Prov(\ulcorner G\urcorner)\supset Prov(\ulcorner \sim G\urcorner)\qquad\text{t-f logic from (2) and (3)}\\
&(5)\quad\vdash Prov(\ulcorner G\urcorner)\supset \sim(Con)\qquad\text{t-f logic from (4) and }(\#)\\
&(6)\quad\vdash (Con)\supset \sim Prov(\ulcorner G\urcorner)\qquad\text{contrapositive of (5)}\\
&(7)\quad\vdash (Con)\supset G\qquad\text{t-f logic from (6) and the fixed point}
\end{aligned}
If (Con) is derivable, then we can derive G. From Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem we know that if G is derivable then PA is not consistent. So (Con) is not derivable.
QED
Löb’s Theorem
We know that G says “I am not provable” is indeed unprovable. Then what about an H says “I am provable”? Consider the fixed point H for the formula Prov that \vdash H\equiv Prov(\ulcorner H\urcorner). Can we prove H? By our intuition there is no conflict if we can derive H. In 1955, Löb settled the matter by an ingenious proof that:


                  
                   Löb's Theorem
                  
                

Let F be a formula such that \vdash Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner) \supset F. Then \vdash F.


Note that here the provability predicate must be a standard one.
Proof:
Let F be a formula such that \vdash Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner) \supset F, and we wish to show that \vdash F. Let H be a fixed point of the formula Prov(y)\supset F, that is
\vdash H\equiv \big( Prov(\ulcorner H\urcorner) \supset F\big)
For convenience, denote the formula Prov(\ulcorner H\urcorner) \supset F by J and the formula Prov(\ulcorner Prov(\ulcorner H\urcorner)\urcorner) by K.
\begin{aligned}
(1)\quad &\vdash H\supset J \qquad\text{fixed point}\\
(2)\quad &\vdash Prov(\ulcorner H\urcorner)\supset Prov(\ulcorner J\urcorner)\qquad\text{Quick FMP of (1)}\\
(3)\quad &\vdash Prov(\ulcorner J\urcorner)\supset \big(K\supset Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner)\big)\qquad\text{FMP}\\
(4)\quad &\vdash Prov(\ulcorner H\urcorner)\supset K  \qquad\text{Formal adequacy}\\
(5)\quad &\vdash Prov(\ulcorner H\urcorner)\supset Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner)  \qquad\text{by t-f logic from (2)},(3),(4)\\
(6)\quad &\vdash Prov(\ulcorner F\urcorner)\supset F\qquad\text{supposition}\\
(7)\quad &\vdash Prov(\ulcorner H\urcorner)\supset F \qquad\text{t-f logic from (5),(6)}\\
(8)\quad &\vdash H \qquad\text{t-f logic from (7) and the fixed point}\\
(9)\quad &\vdash Prov(\ulcorner H\urcorner)\qquad\text{Adequacy of (8)}\\
(10)\quad &\vdash F \qquad\text{t-f logic from (7),(9)}\\
\end{aligned}
QED

Löb’s theorem actually implies the soundness of PA, for if you can prove something, then it is true. (it does not imply we can prove it though, since not every true formula is provable).
Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem then is an easy corollary of Löb’s theorem. Suppose \vdash (Con). Recall that (Con) is \sim Prov(\ulcorner S0 = 0\urcorner ). By t-f logic \vdash Prov(\ulcorner S0=0\urcorner )\supset H for any formula H, then \vdash Prov(\ulcorner S0=0\urcorner )\supset S0=0. By Löb’s theorem \vdash S0=0, so that PA is inconsistent.

phil_public/Intro_2_formal_epistemology.title: Intro_2_formal_epistemology
phil_public/Intro_2_formal_epistemology.content:
metaphysics epistemology
Confirmation
Scientific -testing appears to work something like “deduction in reverse” (Goodman 1954). Like for a hypothesis like All electrons have negative charge, we confirm this hypothesis by observing an a such that Ea and Na, and conclude that \forall x(Ex\supset Nx). Intuitively, the confirmation is strengthened if we verify with b and c.
These observations suggest a proposal due to Nicod (1930) and famously examined by Hempel (1945):
Nicod’s Criterion
A universal generalization is confirmed by its positive instances (as long as no counter-instances are discovered): \forall x(Fx\supset Gx) is confirmed by Fa\wedge Ga, by Fb\wedge Gb, etc.
One classic challenge for Nicod’s criterion is the notorious raven paradox.
Since \forall x(Fx\supset Gx)\equiv \forall x(\sim Gx\supset \sim Fx), then for the hypothesis that all ravens are black, why cannot a non-black non-raven confirm the hypothesis?
Intuitively, it was due to the different size of the sample. 
Another challenge was to consider the hypothesis: Only half of all the ravens are black. Then even if you survey large numbers of ravens, you could still say maybe the rest are non-black.
Law of large numbers?
The challenge suggests important lessons: 1. We need a laxer notion of prediction than deduction; 2. Confirmation is quantitative; 3. Degrees of confirmation should be understood in terms of probability.
Probability Approach
Standard theory begins with a function p, which takes in a proposition and returns a number x, the probability of the proposition: p(A) = x. To qualify as a probability function, p must satisfy three axioms:
For any proposition A, 0\le p(A)\le 1.
For any tautology A, p(A) = 1.
For any logically incompatible propositions A and B, p(A\vee B) = p(A)+p(B).
The conditional probability of B given A is written p(B\mid A) and is defined:
	p(B\mid A) = \frac{p(A\wedge B)}{p(A)}
Introduce the degree of confirmation, which E confirms H, written c(H,E) is defined as:
c(H,E) = p(H\mid E)- p(H).
When c(H,E)<0, we say it disconfirms the hypothesis. When c(H,E) = 0, we say E is neural to H .
Other theorems:
No chance for contradiction: When A is a contradiction, p(A) = 0.
Complementarity for Contradiction: For any A, p(A) = 1-p(\sim A).
Equality for Equivalence: When A and B are logically equivalent, p(A) = p(B).
Conditional Certainty for Logical Consequences: When A logically entails B, p(B\mid A) = 1.
Conjunction Costs Probability: For any A and B, p(A)\le p(A\wedge B), the equivalence holds when p(A\wedge\sim B) = 0.
Conjunction Rule: For any A and B that p(B)\neq 0, p(A\wedge B) = p(A\mid B)p(B).
The Law of Total Probability: For any A and B that probability is neither 0 or 1:
p(A) = p(A\mid B)p(B)+p(A\mid \sim B)p(\sim B).

Baye’s Theorem
This theorem relates a conditional probability p(H\mid E) to the unconditional probability p(H):
p(H\mid E) = p(H)\,\frac{p(E\mid H)}{p(E)}
What’s the philosophical significance of Bayes’ theorem? It unifies a number of influential ideas about confirmation and scientific methodology, binding them together in a single, simple equation.

Theoretical Fit. It’s a truism that the better a theory fits the evidence (bigger p(E\mid H)), the more the evidence supports it.
Novel Prediction. Another truism is that novel predictions count more. (smaller p(E))
Prior Plausibility. A final truism: new evidence for a theory has to be weighed against the theory’s prior plausibility (p(H)).


Now reconsider the raven’s paradox. Given predicates that R being “being raven”, B being “being black”, H being the hypothesis that “All ravens are black”.
Theorem (Raven Theorem): If 1. p(\sim R\mid \sim B) is very high and 2. p(\sim B\mid H) = p(\sim B), then p(H\mid \sim R\wedge \sim B) is just slightly larger than p(H).
POI and induction problem
The Principle of Indifference (PoI):
Given n mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive possibilities, none of which is favored over the others by the available evidence, the probability of each is 1/n.
Subjectivists believe initial probability assignments are reasonable, allowing for both inductive optimism and skepticism.
Objectivists argue for a single, correct way to assign probabilities, often using the Principle of Indifference, though interpretations vary on its consistency and dependence on possibility divisions.

Consider the case when you flip ten coins in a row. If the first nine came out to be tails, does it matter to your judgement of the tenth? In fact, if calculate based on conditional probability, we know the possibility of the last toss is 50-50 (events are independent). However, this knowledge was not given by the axiom of the probability.

phil_public/Notes_on_basic_FOL.title: Notes_on_basic_FOL
phil_public/Notes_on_basic_FOL.content:
based on Introduction to Mathematical Logic
Model theory
As a preliminary step, for a given s in \Sigma we shall define a function s^{*} that assigns to each term t of \mathcal{L} an elements s^{*}(t) in D:
1. If t is a variablex_{j}, let s^{*}(t) be s_{j}
2.  If t is an individual constant a_{j}, then s^{*}(t) is the interpretation (a_{j})^{M} of this constant.
3. If f_{k}^{n} is a function letter, (f_{k}^{n})^{M} is the corresponding operation in D, and t_{1},\dots,t_{n} are terms, then s^{*}(f_{k}^{n}(t_{1},\dots,t_{n})) = (f_{k}^{n})^{M}(s^{*}(t_{1}),\dots,s^{*}(t_{n}))
Inductive definition of satisfaction:
1. If \mathscr{B} is an atomic wf A^{n}_{k}(t_{1},\dots,t_{n}) and (A_{k}^{n})^{M} is the corresponding n-place relation of the interpretation, then a sequence s=(s_{1},s_{2},\dots) satisfies \mathscr{B} iff (A_{k}^{n})^{M}(s^{*}(t_{1}),\dots,s^{*}(t_{n})), that is to say the n-place sequence \langle s^{*}(t_{1}),\dots,s^{*}(t_{n})\rangle is in the relation (A_{k}^{n})^{M}.
2. s satisfies \lnot\mathscr B iff s does not satisfies \mathscr B.
3. s satisfies \mathscr B\Rightarrow\mathscr C iff s does not satisfy \mathscr B or s satisfies \mathscr C.
4. s satisfies (\forall x_{i})\mathscr B iff every sequence that differs from s in at most the i-th component satisfies \mathscr B
Definitions
1. A wf \mathscr B is true for the interpretation M (written \models_{M}\mathscr B) iff every sequence in \Sigma satisfies \mathscr B.
2. \mathscr B is said to be false for M iff no sequence in \Sigma satisfies \mathscr B.
3. An interpretation M is said to be a model for a set \Gamma of wfs iff every wf in \Gamma is true for M.
Notes
\models_{M}\mathscr B iff \models_{M}(\forall x_{j})\mathscr B
By the closure of \mathscr B we mean the closed wf obtained from \mathscr B by prefixing in universal quantifiers those variables, in order of descending subscripts, that are free in \mathscr B. If \mathscr B has no free variables, the closure of \mathscr B is defined to be \mathscr B itself. e.g. take \mathscr B as A_{1}^{2}(x_{2},x_{5})\Rightarrow \lnot(\exists x_{2})A_{1}^{3}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}), its closure is (\forall x_{5})(\forall x_{3})(\forall x_{2})(\forall x_{1})\mathscr B. Then a wf \mathscr B is true iff its closure is true.
Every instance of a tautology is true for ANY interpretation. e.g. an instance of A_{1}\Rightarrow \lnot A_{2}\lor A_{1} is A_{1}^{1}(x_{2})\Rightarrow\big(\lnot(\forall x_{1})A_{1}^{1}(x_{1})\big)\lor A_{1}^{1}(x_{2}).
If the free variables of a wf \mathscr B occur in the list x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{k}} and if the sequence s and s' have the same components in the i_{1}th, …, i_{k}th places, then s satisfies \mathscr B iff s' satisfies \mathscr B. e.g. A_1^1(x_2)\lor \exists x_5\,A_2^2(x_5,x_2) has the only free variable x_{2}, then as long as in the sequence s and s', s_{2}=s'_{2}, s\models_{M}\mathscr B\Longleftrightarrow s'\models_{M}\mathscr B. (VIII)
If \mathscr B is a closed wf of a language \mathscr L, then for any interpretation of M, either \models_{M}\mathscr B or \models_{M}\mathscr \lnot B. (of course \mathscr B may be true for some interpretations and false for others)
If \mathscr B is not closed, that is \mathscr B has free variables, it may be neither true nor false for some interpretation.
sketch of proof For any fixed interpretation M, there are two situations. First, exists s such that s\models_{M}\mathscr B. Since \mathscr B is closed, then by (VIII), we know that for any s, s\models_{M}\mathscr B.
Second, there is no s such that s\models_{M}\mathscr B, then for all s, s\not\models_{M}\mathscr B, that is \mathscr B is false, then \lnot \mathscr B is true, so s\models_{M}\mathscr \lnot B.
Assume t is free for x_{i} in \mathscr B(x_{i}). Then (\forall x_{i})\mathscr B(x_{i})\Rightarrow \mathscr B(t) is true for all interpretations.
If \mathscr B does not contain x_{i} free, then (\forall x_{i})(\mathscr B\Rightarrow \mathscr C)\Rightarrow(\mathscr B\Rightarrow (\forall x_{j})\mathscr C).
Lemma 1
If t and u are terms, s is a sequence in \Sigma, t' results from t by replacing all occurrences of x_{i} by u, and s' results from s by replacing the i-th component of s by s^{*}(u), then s^{*}(t') = (s')^{*}(t).
Lemma 2
Let t be free for x_{i} in \mathscr B(x_{i}). Then:
1. A sequences s = (s_{1},s_{2},\dots) satisfies \mathscr B(t) iff the sequence s', obtained from s by substituting s^{*}(t) for s_{i} in the i-th place, satisfies \mathscr B(x_{i}).
2. If (\forall x_{i})\mathscr B(x_{i}) is satisfied by the sequences s, then \mathscr B(t) also satisfied by s.
Definitions
logically valid wf \mathscr B: \mathscr B is true for every interpretation
\mathscr B satisfiable iff there is an interpretation for which \mathscr B is satisfied by at least one sequence
If \mathscr B is a closed wf, then \mathscr B is either true or false for any given interpretation, i.e. \mathscr B is satisfied by all sequences or none.
A set \Gamma of wfs is said to be satisfiable iff there is an interpretation where there is a sequence that satisfies every wf of \Gamma.

phil_public/PA.title: PA
phil_public/PA.content:
math_logic
see formal_system before this
Based on \mathcal L_{S}, add new signs: '+' and '\times'. New formation rules:
1. 0 is a term; each formal variable is a term
2. If s and t are terms then so are St, (s+t), and (s\times t).
New axioms:
Number-theoretical axioms of PA
\begin{align}
&\sim Sx = 0 \tag{N1}\\
&Sx = Sy \supset x = y \tag{N2}\\
&x + 0 = x \tag{N3}\\
&x + Sy = S(x + y) \tag{N4}\\
&x \times 0 = 0 \tag{N5}\\
&x \times Sy = (x \times y) + x \tag{N6}\\
&F(0) \land \forall x\big(F(x) \supset F(Sx)\big) \supset \forall x\,F(x) \tag{N7}
\end{align}
Note that N7 is a schema. It is not appropriate to say that \Sigma_{PA} has 7 axioms - it has infinitely many because of N7, the mathematical induction schema.
We can prove every arithmetical laws in PA.

phil_public/formal_system.title: formal_system
phil_public/formal_system.content:
math_logic
Certain symbols and rules form a formal language. Formal languages with certain axioms are formal systems. 
\mathcal{L_{=}} and \Sigma_{=}
There are six signs in the language of \mathcal{L_{=}}. '=', '\sim', '\supset', '\forall', '(', ')' along with formal variables, 'x', 'y', 'z' and such and such. The formation rules are as follows:
1. If u and v are formal variables, then u=v is a formula.
2. If F and G are formulas, then \sim F and (F\supset G) are formulas
3. If F is a formula and u is a formal variable, then \forall u (F) is a formula.
Note that in this step we haven’t incorporate anything about how to interpret the language.
A derivation is a finite sequence F1,…,Fn of formulas such that each formula in the sequence either is an axiom or else results by a rule of inference from formulas that precede it in the sequence. We now give the derivation rules for a formal language, \Sigma_{=}, whose formal language is \mathcal{L_{=}}.
Truth-functional axioms
\begin{align}
&F \supset (G\supset F) \tag{T1}\\
&(F\supset(G\supset H))\supset((F\supset G)\supset(F\supset H))\tag{T2}\\
&(F\supset G)\supset(\sim G\supset\sim F)\tag{T3}\\
&F\supset\sim\sim F\tag{T4}\\
&\sim\sim F\supset F\tag{T5}
\end{align}
Note that we cannot derive truth table from this axioms, for it is merely a syntactical process, not semantical.
Quantificational axioms
\begin{align}
&\forall u(F)\supset F'\tag{Q1}\\
&\forall (G\supset F)\supset (G\supset\forall F)\tag{Q2}
\end{align}
Axioms of identity
\begin{align}
&x=x\tag{I1}\\
&x=y\supset(F\supset G)\text{, where }F\text{ and }G \text{ are any formulas that differ only in that }\\
&G \text{ has free $y$ at some or all places where $F$ has free $x$}\tag{I2}
\end{align}
Rules of inference. Let F and G be formulas and u be a variable,
Modus ponens: G maybe inferred from F and F\supset G.
Universal generalization: \forall u F may be inferred from F.
Note that with T1-T5 and modus ponens we can prove all the truth-functionally valid formulas (connect syntax and semantics).
\mathcal{L}_{S} and \Sigma_{S}
Based on \mathcal{L}_{S}, add new sign 0 and S. Add formation rules:
1. '0' is a term, any formal variable is a term.
2. if t is a term, then so is St.
Inherit the 1-3 formation rules of \mathcal{L}_{S}, and change the first one to:
if s and t are terms, then s=t is a formula.
The axioms of successor are as follows:
\begin{align}
& \sim Sx=0\tag{S1}\\
& Sx=Sy \supset x=y\tag{S2}\\
& \sim x=0\supset \exists y (x=Sy)\tag{S3}\\
& \sim S\dots Sx = x\text{, where $'S\dots S'$ represents any nonempty string}\\&\text{of successive occurrences of $'S'$}\tag{S4}
\end{align}
General notions
==Syntax==
\Sigma is consistent iff for no formulas F are both F derivable and \sim F derivable.
\Sigma is syntactically complete iff for every sentence F either F or \sim F is derivable.
\Sigma is decidable iff there is a purely mechanical procedure for determining whether any given formula is derivable in \Sigma.
==Semantics==
\Sigma is sound with respect to an interpretation iff every formula derivable in \Sigma is true under that interpretation.
\Sigma is complete with respect to an interpretation iff every formula true under that interpretation is derivable in \Sigma
Note
if there is at least one interpretation with respect to which \Sigma is sound, then \Sigma is consistent; if there is at least one interpretation with respect to which \Sigma is complete, then \Sigma is syntactically complete.
\sim always interprets as negation.

phil_public/horwich_truth_handout.title: horwich_truth_handout
phil_public/horwich_truth_handout.content:
truth metaphysics horwich
In summary, Horwich holds that a true proposition should follow the equivalence schema below:
\ulcorner p \urcorner \text{ is true} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad p
There might be some part I forgot about the quotation mark \ulcorner\urcorner.
Highlighted parts, section 5, and the last section were written by me, while the rest was reorganized Horwich’s handout.
INTRODUCTION
This document is divided into 5 sections.
In section 1, I’ll indicate how deflationary accounts of truth differ from traditional proposals about the nature of truth — and why a deflationary account is preferable.
In section 2, I’ll begin my assessment of which is the better deflationary account of the meaning of “true” — as between, on the one hand,
(i) My use-theoretic, so-called minimalist suggestion, whose heart is the view that the meaning of the English word “true”, when applied to (or denied of) a proposition, consists in the inclination of English speakers to accept instances of the schema: “The proposition that p is true ↔ p” — which is known as the Equivalence Schema.
And on the other hand,
(ii) Wolfgang Künne’s ingenious, but controversial, definition of “x is true” as
(\exists p)((x = p)\wedge p)
which departs from classical logic by invoking quantification into sentence positions.
It’s worth noting that my above qualification of “the meaning of the English word ‘true’,” by the addition of “when applied to (or denied of) propositions” is essential: because the English word “true” is ambiguous — sometimes used with a meaning that’s very far from the one that my minimalism and Künne’s definition are aiming to capture.
For example, one might say, “She’s a true friend” and “He was a true hero”, where what’s meant (roughly speaking) is “She’s a paradigmatic, or perfect example of a friend” and “He was a paradigmatic, or perfect example of a hero”. But when we describe a certain proposition as true, we are never saying that it’s a perfect, or paradigmatic example of a proposition!!
In section 3, I’ll respond to a valuably challenging essay by the late Sten Lindström, in which he maintains that my Minimalism is substantially inadequate, because of the many truth-claims that it cannot accommodate (or so he argues — but I disagree!)
After that — in the relatively short 4th section of the paper — I turn to the question of whether either of the proposals we have been considering — mine or Künne’s — can accommodate the plausible view that a statement that’s untranslatable into our language might nonetheless be true.
In Section 5 I describe and address a paradox that arises from applying the above-mentioned Equivalence Schema — “The proposition that p is true ↔ p”, to a person’s assertion that what s/he is asserting is not true.
And finally — in light of those discussions — I’ll offer (in section 6) my answers to some provocative questions posed in the announcement of the University of Vienna’s last-September conference on TRUTH:

Is truth definable?
Is propositional quantification coherent?
Do natural languages involve propositional quantification, and in what sense?
What do the answers to these questions mean for philosophical attempts to define or explain truth?


SECTION 1 previous trials
Each of the proposed traditional accounts of truth took the form of a definition that purported to articulate (i) the meaning of the English word “true” (when it’s predicated of propositions), and (ii) the underlying nature of the property of being true.
Here are some prominent examples of such proposed definitions — each one followed by the grounds for rejecting it:

1. “x is true ↔ x corresponds to a fact”
But: the concept of “correspondence” is itself mysterious, yet unexplained.
And — even worse — it’s arguable that the term of itself — the word “fact”, should be defined as “true proposition”! — In which case 1. defines “true” in terms of itself — which is absurd!!
Tim Maudlin tells me that deflationism is just another kind of correspondence theory. We can revisit this argument later.
To see more about correspondence theory, go check [plato.stanford.edu/entries/truth/#CorRev]. 

The correspondence theory of truth expresses the very natural idea that truth is a content-to-world or word-to-world relation: what we say or think is true or false in virtue of the way the world turns out to be.

Correspondence theory is a very natural way of thinking of the truth as a content-to-world relation.

2. “x is true ↔ the possibility articulated by x is actualized”
But surely, a possibility is simply a proposition (one that could be true).
And calling a proposition “actualized” is just an awkward way of saying that it’s true!!

3. Putnam “x is true ↔ a rational investigation would dictate believing x.”

 There Putnam glosses truth as what would be justified under ideal epistemic conditions. With the pragmatists, Putnam sees the ideal conditions as something which can be approximated, echoing the idea of truth as the end of inquiry. (SEP)

But many truths are inaccessible to our investigations — either too remote, or too deep, or too complex, or too conceptually-alien.
And rational considerations often point away from the truth!
Moreover: rational considerations rarely deliver certainty. And being 90% confident in the truth of 100 independent hypotheses implies that their conjunction is probably false!

4. “x is true ↔ x is almost universally believed”
But: surely everyone could agree on a given point, yet all be mistaken.
Consensus can change over time.
And when people are divided, one of them must be right — but the true one is not almost universally believed.

5. Peirce “x is true ↔ x will be believed in the limit of enquiry.”
But: disagreements may never be ironed out.
Agreement in the very distant future cannot ground truth-claims now.
And even permanent agreement cannot guarantee correctness.

6. William James “x is true ↔ decisions based on assuming x will promote practical success.”
But: actions based on a person’s true beliefs can (unluckily) have catastrophic consequences.
Conversely, false beliefs can (luckily) have life-saving consequences.
James’ idea captures something about the value of true beliefs, but cannot define truth.

5. Foucault “x is true ↔ x is what the political powers pressure us to believe.”
But: political powers often pressure us to believe what is false.
And many matters are ones the regime does not care about.
Power may determine what is taken to be true, but not what is true.

SECTION 2 Künne’s schema
Regarding the two deflationary accounts of truth — mine and Künne’s — I’m confident that almost everyone here is prepared to bet that I will proceed by standing up for my own view, and by criticizing Professor Künne’s view.
But those people would lose their money!!
For I don’t share the common complaint about Künne’s account:

that quantification into sentence positions is unintelligible.
or the implied view that classical logic, with quantifiers

“(\forall x)(Fx)” for “everything is F”
“(\exists x)(Fx)” for “something is F”
there are no sentences of ordinary language, whose logical forms are best captured by quantifying into sentence positions.



On the contrary, quantifying into declarative sentence positions is easy to understand and quite useful.
The term “declarative” is inserted here to make it clear that Künne does not endorse quantification into the position of sentences that are questions like “is the window open?” or imperatives like “open the window!” but only into the positions of sentences that express propositions like “the window is open.”
It is easy to understand quantification in positions of declarative sentences. Consider the excluded middle rule (\forall p) (p\vee \sim p), and to be disposed to accept the schema is to be disposed to accept any instance of the schema p\vee \sim p.
Similarly, for the case of truth, we shall recognize that a person’s disposition to accept instances of the equivalence schema \ulcorner p \urcorner \text{ is true}\Leftrightarrow p amounts to his/her being disposed to accept (\forall p) (\ulcorner p \urcorner \text{ is true}\Leftrightarrow p)
As for Künne’s proposed definition of “true:
(\forall x)\bigg(x\text{ is true}\Leftrightarrow (\exists p)(x = \ulcorner p\urcorner \wedge p)\bigg)
I have just offered a defense of Künne’s quantifying with a universal quantifier, into sentence positions. But one might worry that this could not help us to understand his definition of truth, since that definition involves existential quantification into a sentence position.
It could be easily dispelled by propositional logic, and we can turn the statement
(\exists p)(x = \ulcorner p\urcorner \wedge p) into
\sim(\forall p)\bigg(\sim (x = \ulcorner p\urcorner \wedge p)\bigg)
So the disposition to accept Künne’s equivalence schema consists in the pair of dispositions.
Given acceptance of ”x is true” and "x = \ulcorner p \urcorner" to accept p. And given acceptance of some instance of the schema "x = \ulcorner p\urcorner \wedge p" to accept ”x is true”.
Comments： I do not understand what he is talking about in the matter of logic. If we restricted the language to formal language like PA, it could be totally understandable, since we could stipulate the axioms as true propositions. However, here I think every reader would either think the equivalence schema is trivially right or that it says nothing because no instance of true propositions can be enumerated with the guidance of the schema.
Horwich, in fact, I think he would respond like, saying that you cannot define truth, but it still has a meaning. Like you say, snow is white is true. For sure, it is true because snow is white. Once you have accepted that snow is white, you have to accept that it is true. We can check the following examples he gave.
Since I didn’t think Horwich explained it clearly in class, I would show some of my interpretations of his theory later.

SECTION 3 objections
Sten Lindström suggested my approach cannot explain how we might arrive at truth-claims such as:
(a) The Continuum Hypothesis is true.
(b) There are true propositions that aren’t supported by available evidence.
(c) Every sentence is such that either it or its negation is true.
(d) Most statements that Clinton made in his deposition were true.
And I must concede that minimalism lacks the resources to rearticulate any of those truth-claims without using the word “true.”
But Künne’s definition, by contrast, can rearticulate (a) and (b) but not (c) and (d).
But the minimalist has other resources: though we can’t define these claims without “true,” we can explain how we arrive at them.

For example, to reach (a):
We identify the Continuum Hypothesis, and we accept:
“ is the Continuum Hypothesis ↔ p”.
Thus by Leibniz’s Law we infer:
“The Continuum Hypothesis is true.”
Comments:  One may hold that he actually says nothing. The explanation was based on an extremely important premise, that is, one shall accept the continuum hypothesis.
We have to acknowledge that Horwich’s intention was to give nothing epistemic, no commitment to maths, no commitment to science, no commitment metaphysically to the world. However, he would claim that you shall accept the equivalence schema, and truth is governed by instances of the schema.
meaning of truth
relation_to_putnam

Similarly for (b):
Consider a proposition A which is neither supported nor unsupported by any evidence.
Thus at least one propositions are true and unsupported by evidence, that is:
A\,\vee\sim A
Comments: sophistry

For (c):
Start by accepting many instances:
Either A or \sim A,
Either B or \sim B, etc.
Generalize to:
“Every declarative (= proposition-expressing) sentence is such that either it, or its negation, is true.”
Comments: this is more like a correspondence theory. What I was thinking was taking the language where there is an excluded middle rule, which can be related to Putnam and Carnap as well.

For (d):
Find statements ,A_1,\,A_2.\,\dots , that Clinton made.
Determine which are true, then count how many.
SECTION 4 different languages
The issue here is how the two approaches under present consideration — mine and Künne’s — deal with the prospect of true statements articulated using sentences that aren’t translatable into our language.
For simplicity, let’s imagine that we understand nothing but English.
Suppose F is a language, many of whose sentences are not translatable into English.
But suppose F contains an operator, “\{Y\}”, that, when applied to any categorical sentence of F — e.g. FS(k) — yields a singular term, “\{Y\}(FS(k))”, which, like an English that-clause, refers to the proposition expressed by FS(k).
In that case, it could be that language F contains a word — perhaps “fooo” — whose meaning is the same as the English “true”.
For it could be that F-speakers are disposed to accept, for every p, instances of:
\{FS(n)\}\text{ is fooo} \Leftrightarrow FS(n)
And, if so, then the way that F-speakers use their word fooo is the same as the way in which English speakers use “true” — which is our disposition to accept instances of “the proposition that p is true \Leftrightarrow p”.
Presumably, some of F’s untranslatable-into-English sentences might be true.
But English speakers will not be able to tell whether or not this is so.
For only if we could translate FS(k) could we formulate the instance of our equivalence schema that would enable us to specify the truth-condition of FS(k).
And Künne’s definition of “x is true” couldn’t solve this problem either; for it will be impossible for us to tell whether or not:
(\exists p)\bigg( \{FS(k) \} = \ulcorner p\urcorner \wedge p  \bigg)
Comments: Frankly, I acknowledge Horwich’s argument that it is impossible for us to tell whether or not FS(k) is true. The answer is trivial because it is not English (or any other language that we perceive). In Künne’s schema, if we take the "=" just as the identity, then p is in F and if there is a way for us to know whether p holds, we can say that FS(k) is fooo in F, and true (in English) according to the biconditional. I think the result quite conforms to our intuition.
However, in Horwich’s schema, we have to take a step back and only commit to \{FS(n)\}\text{ is fooo} \Leftrightarrow FS(n).
In this sense, Künne’s truth holds across different languages, that is, he can assert the truth inside a language L with another language L', while Horwich can only assert the truth inside the language L by L. If I am right, then Künne’s truth has a more general meaning (if we regard it as merely a meaning, not definition) than Horwich’s. (haven't been discussed)
SECTION 5 Liar paradox
(Horwich’s writing was really messy, and I am rewriting in a relatively more formal way.)
Consider proposition p :
p\Leftrightarrow \ulcorner p \urcorner\text{ is false}
Of course, one could refute that such a self-inference could be illegitimate, but we have to acknowledge that in ordinary languages (English), such self-inferences are inevitable (because the language is too strong). Not to mention, in formal systems, you can even devise a self-inference by diag (PA).
Then consider the equivalence schema, we will get \ulcorner p\urcorner \text{ is true} \Leftrightarrow p, which is
\ulcorner p\urcorner \text{ is true} \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad  \ulcorner p \urcorner\text{ is false}
Now we infer that p is both true and not true.
Horwich thinks that at least one of our assumptions must be given up. It could be “every contradiction is false”, or the above p doesn’t express a proposition.
Or alternatively, the assumption that every instance of the schema must be accepted.

It seems to me that this last alternative is the best way of escaping from the paradox. — For remember that minimalism’s meaning-theory demands no more than an inclination to accept instances of the equivalence schema. And in this case, the inclination is overwhelmed by the paradoxical consequences of accepting it.

Comments: I don’t like Horwich’s picture for two reasons. (Notice here I don’t mean he is not coherent, I just think it is not that minimalistic as he or I expected). 
First, the disposal of the liar paradox indicates the redundancy in his theory. He didn’t explicitly introduce meta-language to defuse the liar paradox, but implicitly used an operational meta-language. He suggests that we should exclude some instances of the equivalence schema, where the operation “exclude” can only happen in a meta-language outside the object language where we were asserting truth. Then the problem arises if we contemplate the object language, for Horwich never said what the object language is. Is it PA? Is it SA? Or is it just ordinary language? If we add different language frameworks into the consideration (it is very natural if you are a minimalist like Horwich, because you want the truth to be perceived as easy as possible, so you can adjust your meta-language according to your object language), we might collapse into truth pluralism. Therefore, truth loses its status as a unified, stable, meaningful (this word is controversial though) concept.
Second, even though we fix the object language, merely denying that every instance conforms to the schema seems to cause more issues, for there are no clear instructions on which instance we shall give up the schema. One may say, the paradoxical propositions are countable since the words are finite in English (here and the discussion below can be related to an analogue of PA computability). However, Kripke has demonstrated that there is no algorithm to enumerate the paradoxical propositions recursively; that is, whether or not a sentence is paradoxical is not decidable. Then I would say the equivalence schema, as well as the operational meta-language, is flawed and leaky, since we don’t even know when the schema can not be applied.
SECTION 6 answer to 5 questions
Here are my answers to the 5 questions posed in the announcement of Vienna’s September 2024 conference on TRUTH.

Is truth definable?
The word “truth” is the name of the monadic property that’s attributed to a proposition when we predicate “true” of it. And properties aren’t objects of definition.
So I suspect the intended question is:
“Is the English word ‘true’ definable?”
What’s implied by an affirmative answer is that a good definition can be devised, where the potential disqualifying defects include:

reliance on a term (in the proposed defining expression) that’s no less in need of definition than “true” is, or
The proposed defining expression includes a term (e.g. “fact”) that’s pretty clearly defined in terms of “true.”

I think the best candidate for a good definition of “true” is Wolfgang Künne’s.
But one might well feel that its quality depends on whether a clarifying definition of “proposition” can be provided.
However, I must concede that the absence of any such clarification of “proposition” would count against my minimalist proposal no less than it counts against Wolfgang’s definition of “true”.
Remarks: Russel denied the existence of the proposition, but I am not sure whether it was in Horwich’s sense.
Horwich said to me multiple times that he doesn’t want an (analytic) definition for truth, and he thinks pursuing definitions leads to infinite regress. Therefore, he thinks we shall choose truth as the concept that has a meaning without definition to end the regress. (And meaning is just use, in a Wittgenstein’s sense)
What is most important here is that we have to understand that in this picture, there is no metaphysical commitment to truth; that is, the schema itself won’t give any more knowledge (or knowledge of knowledge) about the cognitive object. What else he would say may probably (given by GPT):

Truth is a logical tool, not a property of reality;
The equivalence schema is meaning-constitutive
You learn the meaning of “true” by learning a rule:
	Anytime you accept 𝑝, you are also inclined to accept “𝑝 is true”.


Is propositional quantification coherent?
Obviously, we can coherently quantify over propositions — e.g.:
“There is a proposition expressed by the English sentence, ‘Snow is white’ ”
Or in other words:
“(\existsx)(x is a proposition \wedge x is expressed in English by ‘Snow is white’).”
So I assume that the intended question is:
“Is it coherent to quantify into declarative-sentence positions?”
And to this very different question, my answer is also “YES.”
For, as I suggested in Section 2, it’s plausible that our acceptance of:
(\exists p)(\#...p)
consists in our acceptance of the instance of (\#...p).

metaphysics explanation induction
Intro
The chief task:

a clarification and definition of the concept of the degree of confirmation
a clarification of the logical nature of induction and a construction of a system of inductive logic
a clarification of the concept of probability

On explication

The explicatum(explication) must fulfill the requirements of similarity to the explicandum(stuff being explained), exactness, fruitfulness, and simplicity. (1)



The explicatum must be given by explicit rules for its use, for example, by a definition which incorporates it into a well-constructed system of scientific concepts, either logical, mathematical, or empirical concepts. (3)


Carnap suggests that there are three concepts that provide effective tools for a more penetrating analysis of explication.

Classificatory concepts are those that serve for the classification of things or cases into two or a few mutually exclusive kinds.
Quantitative concepts are those which serve for characterizing things or events or certain of their features by the ascription of numerical values.
Comparative concepts serve for the formulation of the result of a comparison in the form of a more-less-statement without the use of numerical values.

Classificatory concepts are the simplest and least effective kinds of concept, and comparative concepts are more powerful; quantitative concepts are the most powerful. Consider the example of describing temperature: at the early stage of the language, we have classificatory words like “warm” and “cold”; later, we introduce comparative words like “warmer”; finally, we have quantitative words like temperature.
Carnap thinks the concept of Temperature can be regarded as an explicatum for the comparative concept “warmer” (12).

Remarks on the requirements of similarity:

The requirements refer to most cases, but not all cases. Take the example of temperature, the requirement of similarity could be affected by personal experience (like the feeling of hotness may contradict the measurement). However, Carnap explained that we are accustomed to letting the scientific concept overrule the prescientific one in all cases of disagreement, and therefore, the term “warmer” has undergone a change of meaning to “warmer*“. (based on this explanation I don’t really get why the requirements is not for all cases)
The direction from the prescientific sense to the scientific sense is not required. The similar heat sensation (prescientific) does not reject the concept of Temperature (scientific)
There are two scientific concepts “warmer*” and “Temperature”. We first have prescientific sensation to guide us and once the scientific concept is determined we follow its guidance in cases where the prescientific concept is not sufficiently discriminative.
Comments: Here Carnap said “it would be possible but highly inadvisable to define a concept Temperature in such a way that x and y are said to have the same temperature whenever our sensations do not show a difference.” Actually, it remains a problem whether we can define scientifically according to our sensations. In the above sense, it would be “feel-like temperature”.
Quantitative concepts don't imply fruitfulness and vice versa. Warmer* can be defined in a non-quantitative way (Carnap gave an example on 14) and is adequate for an explicatum.
Comments: it seems that explicatum was linked to a certain kind of phenomenology…maybe I will return to this later in the discussion of confirmation.

Formalization and Interpretation
Carnap separates the language of science into two steps: formalization and interpretation.

The two steps are the two phases of what is known as the axiomatic (or postulational) method in its modern form. (15)

The former step is constructing a formal (axiomatized) system for a concept or a theory. The latter step is given by the rules specifying the meanings for terms in a formal system, and hence the rules are of a semantic nature or epistemic correlations.
Take PA as an example.

…the ordinary theorems of elementary arithmetic terms can be proved. In this procedure, the primitive terms mentioned and the terms introduced on their basis remain uninterpreted. It is only for didactic, psychological reasons that not arbitrarily chosen symbols are taken as primitive terms, but customary signs or words.
…it does not yet reach an explication of the arithmetical terms ‘one’, ‘two’, ‘plus’… In order to do this, an interpretation must be given for the semiformal axiom system. There is an infinite number of true interpretations for this system. (17)
He mentioned that the explication was done by Frege and Russel.


intends to examine a certain hypothesis h; he makes many observations of particular events which he regards as relevant for judging the hypothesis h; he formulates the results of all observations made or as many of them as are relevant in a report, which is a long sentence. Then he tries to determine whether and to what degree the hypothesis h is confirmed by the observational evidence e. This last question alone is what we shall be concerned with. We call it a logical question because, once a hypothesis is formulated by h and any possible evidence by e (it need not be the evidence actually observed), the problem of whether and how much h is confirmed by e is to be answered merely by a logical analysis of h and e and their relations…Once h and e are given, the question mentioned requires only that we be able to understand them, that is, to grasp their meanings, and to establish certain relations which are based upon their meanings. Since we take semantics as the theory of the meanings of expressions in language and especially of sentences, then relations between h and e to be studied may be characterized as semantical; therefore we call them semantical concepts of confirmation.

Carnap then emphasized that the question of confirmation is of inductive logic, not deductive logic. 
Two concepts of probability

the conception of probability as a certain objective logical relation between propositions
the conception of probability as relative frequency


This multiplicity of phrases shows that any assumption of a unique explicandum common to all authors is untenable.


Probability_{1} is relative to a given evidence and that therefore a complete statement of probability_{1} must contain a reference to the evidence is very important. (31)

Psychologism in logic
Many logicians prefer formulations which may be regarded as a kind of qualified psychologism. They admit that logic is not concerned with the actual process of believing, thinking, inferring, because then it would become a part of psychology.
The decisive point to examine is the way in which an author solves his logical problems, demonstrates logical theorems. If here his procedure is objectivistic, that is, free from references to the features of actual processes of thinking, then we have to regard his logic as objectivistic.

phil_public/undefinability_of_i.content:
metaphysics explanation maudlin kripke
This question was raised in Tim Maudlin’s lecture discussing naming and necessity. Tim was arguing that referring to something (especially pointing to something), say pointing to a book and claiming that it is blablabla, is purely an anaphoric chain and nothing causal was involved. Then one gave an instance that the imaginary unit i is not definable, but you can point to it on the complex plane (I guess that was what he was trying to say), which was refuted by Tim.
I found the problem intriguing, though I didn’t understand what they were talking about in the lecture.
Additionally, GPT said Tim was wrong because pointing to something is deictic, not anaphoric.
Here is basically what Tim was saying (in an informal way and some technically wrong because he was mixing the notion of field and ring).
Consider the set of natural numbers \mathbb{N}:\{0,1,2,\dots\}. We know its structure, that there is a special unit 0 which does not have a predecessor, so its successors can be recursively referred to.
For a slightly more complicated set \mathbb Z:\{\dots,-2,-1,0,1,2,\dots\}. There is no such special unit in the above sense. However, consider the operation + and \times are defined so we can refer to 0 as the special unit in the binary operation 0+x = x and 0\times x = x (in a very informal way). Nevertheless, Tim claimed that due to the symmetry of the two operations, we cannot distinguish between the negative numbers and the positive numbers. I was distracted here because I was thinking that, since natural numbers are a semiring, why can’t we distinguish them in this way? (actually a more formal way is to define 1 as the unique multiplicative identity)
The Problem
Now consider the imaginary unit i, and we know that it was defined as:
i = \sqrt{-1}\qquad\text{or}\qquad i^{2} = -1
The intuition is that, it is indiscernible between i and -i since (-i)^{2}= -1 as well. You might say we can draw it on the complex plane, but simply mirroring the plane (or change the direction of the axis) does no harm. That is to say, given two distinct mathematical objects (that is weird I don’t know why we must regard them as distinct ones), though we refer to them in the name of i and -i, we do not intrinsically know which object is truly (this word is problematic though) the i.
Undefinability in Model Theory
In model theory, a structure M (like \mathbb C) interprates a formal language L (like the language of fields).
A subset S\subseteq M^n is called definable if there is a formula \varphi(x_1,\dots,x_n) in L such that:
S = \{ (a_1,\dots,a_n) \in M^n : M \models \varphi(a_1,\dots,a_n)\}.
An element a\in M is definable if there is a formula \varphi(x) with exactly one solution in M, i.e has unique item preserving the formula true.
For our case, we need a first-order formula \varphi(x) such that:
\mathbb{C} \models \varphi(i) \quad \text{and} \quad \text{for all } a \in \mathbb{C}, \mathbb{C} \models \varphi(a) \rightarrow a = i.
This can be proved by an automorphism, and below is an informal proof.


                  
                  Definition of automorphism (informal) 
                  
                

A homomorphism between two L-structures M and N is a map h : |M| \to |N| that respects the structure:
h(f^M(a_1,\dots,a_n)) = f^N(h(a_1),\dots,h(a_n))
and for every relation symbol R,
(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in R^M \implies (h(a_1),\dots,h(a_n))\in R^N,
and constants are preserved: h(c^M)=c^N.
If the map h is bijective and its inverse is also a homomorphism, it’s an isomorphism.
If it’s an isomorphism from a structure onto itself, it’s an automorphism.


An important corollary is that, an automorphism preserves all the truths. For instance, for the field \mathbb C, any automorphism, say \sigma, preserves the field operation:
\sigma(z+w) = \sigma(z) + \sigma(w), \qquad \sigma(z \cdot w) = \sigma(z) \cdot \sigma(w),
and of course
\sigma(0)=0, \quad \sigma(1)=1.


                  
                  Fact 
                  
                

If a is definable (without parameters), then every automorphism of M fixes a


This fact is obvious from the above corollary, which suggests that
M \models \varphi(a) \implies M \models \varphi(f(a)),
and by uniqueness f(a) = a.


                  
                  Proposition 
                  
                

The imaginary unit i is not definable in \mathbb C.




                  
                  Proof 
                  
                

Consider the automorphism \sigma(a+bi) = a-bi, i.e. conjugation. The automorphism fixes only the real numbers. If i were definable in the language of field, then \sigma(i) = i, but according to the definition \sigma(i) = -i \neq i, contradicted.
